guide.title: Flaminio, Rome: MAXXI, the Teatro Olimpico and the left bank of the Tiber
guide.intro: Flaminio is a quartiere on the left bank of the Tiber, outside the Aurelian Walls. Rome numbers its quartieri and Flaminio is Q. I, the first in that series, with the toponymic code 201; it takes its name from the via Flaminia, the consular road that forms its eastern edge. A quartiere is a far larger unit than a rione, and this one is a wedge with a road on one side and a river on the other, which is why several things visitors file under Flaminio stand on the far side of one or the other. What is genuinely here: MAXXI, the national museum of 21st-century art and architecture; the Teatro Olimpico; the sculptor Hendrik Christian Andersen's studio-house, now a state museum; the Navy's Palazzo Marina; the basilica of Santa Croce a Via Flaminia; a disused 19th-century river landing; and three bridges across the Tiber.

sections.heading: The borders of the quartiere
sections.body:
The quartiere's own article gives its borders line by line, and every one of them is a road or the river. To the north and west is Q. XV Della Vittoria, separated by the Tiber in the stretch from ponte Matteotti to ponte Milvio. To the east are Q. II Parioli, separated by piazzale Cardinal Consalvi and by via Flaminia as far as viale Maresciallo Pilsudski, and Q. III Pinciano, separated by via Flaminia from viale Maresciallo Pilsudski to piazzale Flaminio. To the south is the rione Campo Marzio, separated by the Aurelian Walls along via Luisa di Savoia, from piazzale Flaminio to the river at ponte Matteotti. Via Flaminia is that eastern boundary along its whole length.

Flaminio is therefore a left-bank quartiere. The Foro Italico, the Stadio dei Marmi and the Stadio Olimpico are across the river in Della Vittoria. Two buildings that carry the name stand outside it as well: the Stadio Flaminio, whose own article says that despite the name the stadium belongs administratively to the quartiere Parioli, and the Palazzetto dello Sport, whose own article says it stands in the quartiere Parioli. The Auditorium Parco della Musica is in Parioli too. One thing under it is not: the Sovrintendenza Capitolina, which runs the site's museum, opens its own account with the words «Nel quartiere Flaminio, durante i lavori per la realizzazione dell'Auditorium progettato da Renzo Piano, nel 1995 vennero alla luce i resti di una grande villa suburbana».

Piazzale Flaminio is described by its own source as a square divided between the quartieri Pinciano and Flaminio, so no zone owns it. Porta del Popolo, Piazza del Popolo, the fountains around it, the Obelisco Flaminio and Santa Maria del Popolo are in the rione Campo Marzio. Ponte Milvio is at the northern limit, and via Flaminia runs to it.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
No source states a metro station or a bus route inside this quartiere, and no walking times or distances are given here. Piazzale Flaminio, where the metro station carrying the quartiere's name stands, is a square divided between Pinciano and Flaminio. Steer by addresses instead.

MAXXI is at via Guido Reni 4/A, 00196, with a second entrance at via Guido Reni 8 serving the bookshop and café; the basilica of Santa Croce a Via Flaminia is on the same street and the two buildings adjoin. The Teatro Olimpico is at piazza Gentile da Fabriano 17, 00196, in a block bounded by piazza Gentile da Fabriano, lungotevere Flaminio, viale del Vignola and via Giorgio Vasari. The Museo Hendrik Christian Andersen is at via Pasquale Stanislao Mancini 20. Palazzo Marina has two main entrances, one on piazza della Marina off via Flaminia and one on lungotevere delle Navi, with a service entrance on via Domenico Alberto Azuni. Piazza Perin del Vaga, 00196, runs between piazza Melozzo da Forlì and the junction of via Girolamo Muziano with via Masolino da Panicale.

Four embankment roads carry most of the addresses on the river side, and each has a stated run. Lungotevere Arnaldo da Brescia runs from via Ferdinando di Savoia to ponte Matteotti, through the rione Campo Marzio and the quartiere Flaminio; the Monumento a Giacomo Matteotti and the Scalo de Pinedo are both addressed to it. Lungotevere delle Navi runs from ponte Giacomo Matteotti to piazzale delle Belle Arti. Lungotevere Flaminio runs from piazzale delle Belle Arti to ponte Duca d'Aosta. Lungotevere Grande Ammiraglio Thaon di Revel runs from ponte Duca d'Aosta to via Flaminia.

sections.heading: Tickets and opening hours
sections.body:
MAXXI's own site gives Tuesday to Sunday 11.00 to 19.00, closed Monday, with the ticket desk closing an hour before the museum. Its published admission is 15 euro at the desk and 14 euro online, 12 euro and 11 euro reduced for ages 18 to 25 and for groups of fifteen or more, and free under 18; a fifteen-day MAXXI Replay ticket costs the same as a full ticket and an open ticket valid a year costs 18 euro. Audio guides are 3 euro, in Italian and English, and the museum is in the Roma Pass circuit. The Piazza Alighiero Boetti, the museum's forecourt, is a separate matter: the same site states that it stays open to the public free of charge, outside the museum's opening hours as well as during them, with works displayed in it.

The Teatro Olimpico's own site gives box-office hours of 9.30 to 13.00 and 14.00 to 18.30, Monday to Friday, and a summer closure from 25 July to 23 August. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina gives free entry, ingresso libero, for the archaeological museum of the villa romana dell'Auditorium.

No current source states the Museo Hendrik Christian Andersen's opening hours or admission prices, so none are given here; the figures that circulate for it come from a ministry page archived in 2007. No source states opening hours for the basilica of Santa Croce a Via Flaminia, for the church of Sant'Andrea del Vignola or for the Oratorio di Sant'Andrea a Ponte Milvio. Palazzo Marina is a working ministry building and no source states public opening hours for it either.

faq.question: Is MAXXI in Flaminio, and what does it cost?
faq.answer: Yes. MAXXI, the national museum of 21st-century art and architecture, is at via Guido Reni 4/A, 00196, and its second entrance at via Guido Reni 8 serves the bookshop and café. Its own site gives Tuesday to Sunday 11.00 to 19.00, closed Monday, with the ticket desk closing an hour earlier, and admission of 15 euro at the desk or 14 euro online, 12 euro and 11 euro reduced for ages 18 to 25 and groups of fifteen or more, free under 18. An open ticket valid a year costs 18 euro and audio guides are 3 euro. The museum is in the Roma Pass circuit.

faq.question: Are the Auditorium Parco della Musica and the Stadio Flaminio in this quartiere?
faq.answer: No. The Auditorium Parco della Musica is in Parioli, and so is the Stadio Flaminio: the stadium's own article states that despite the name it belongs administratively to the quartiere Parioli. The Palazzetto dello Sport is Parioli's on the same kind of evidence. One site in that group does belong here — the Roman villa found in 1995 during the works for the Auditorium, whose museum is run by the Sovrintendenza Capitolina, and whose own page begins by placing it in the quartiere Flaminio.

faq.question: Which bridges are in Flaminio?
faq.answer: Three: ponte Duca d'Aosta, ponte della Musica-Armando Trovajoli and ponte del Risorgimento. Each of them lies in two quartieri, Flaminio on the left bank and Q. XV Della Vittoria on the right. Two others touch the quartiere: ponte Giacomo Matteotti and ponte Pietro Nenni, which cross to the rione Prati, and ponte Milvio, at the northern limit.

faq.question: Can you go inside Palazzo Marina?
faq.answer: It is a working ministry building, owned by the Ministry of Defence and housing the Navy's central library, and no source states public opening hours, so none are given here. From the street, the river-front entrance on lungotevere delle Navi is flanked by the anchors of the Austro-Hungarian battleships Tegetthoff, on the left, and Viribus Unitis, on the right, and the building runs 142 metres long and 28 metres high in brick and travertine.

faq.question: Is anything here free?
faq.answer: Several things. The Piazza Alighiero Boetti at MAXXI is free and stays open outside the museum's own hours, with works displayed in it. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina gives free entry to the archaeological museum of the villa romana dell'Auditorium. And the outdoor part of the quartiere costs nothing: the four embankment roads, the Monumento a Giacomo Matteotti and the Scalo de Pinedo beside it on lungotevere Arnaldo da Brescia, the elliptical pedestrian square of piazza Perin del Vaga with its two travertine dolphin fountains, and the three bridges.

places.name: MAXXI - Museo nazionale delle arti del XXI secolo
places.summary: A national museum of 21st-century art and architecture, in two sections, MAXXI arte and MAXXI architettura, run by the Fondazione MAXXI under the culture ministry. The entrance is at via Guido Reni 4/A; a second entrance at via Guido Reni 8 serves the bookshop and café. The museum's own site gives Tuesday to Sunday 11.00 to 19.00, closed Monday, with the ticket desk closing an hour before the museum. Admission is 15 euro at the desk and 14 euro online, 12 euro and 11 euro reduced for ages 18 to 25 and for groups of fifteen or more, and free under 18; a fifteen-day MAXXI Replay ticket costs the same as a full ticket and an open ticket valid a year costs 18 euro. Audio guides are 3 euro, in Italian and English. The museum is in the Roma Pass circuit.
places.history: The competition was announced in July 1998 by the Soprintendenza Speciale per l'Arte Contemporanea. It drew 273 entries, fifteen of which were shortlisted, and Zaha Hadid's scheme was selected at the end of February 1999; the museum opened in 2010. It was built on the site of the disused ex caserma Montello: the long block beside the basilica of Santa Croce a Via Flaminia and the barracks' via Guido Reni façade survive and are incorporated into the design, and museum and basilica adjoin.

places.name: Piazza Alighiero Boetti
places.summary: The forecourt of MAXXI, on the museum's via Guido Reni side. The museum's own site states that the Piazza Alighiero Boetti is free and stays open to the public outside the museum's opening hours, with works displayed in it.
places.history: No source states a separate institutional history of the square. It is part of the museum complex that opened in 2010.

places.name: Museo Hendrik Christian Andersen
places.address: Via Pasquale Stanislao Mancini 20, Roma RM
places.summary: The studio-house and sculpture collection of the Norwegian-American sculptor and urbanist Hendrik Christian Andersen, at via Pasquale Stanislao Mancini 20. It is a state museum under the culture ministry, run through the Polo museale del Lazio from December 2014 and through the Direzione Musei statali di Roma from December 2019. No current source states the museum's opening hours or admission prices, so none are given here.
places.history: Andersen built the house to his own design between 1922 and 1925: a palazzina with an attached sculpture studio, its neo-Renaissance elevations carrying heads of members of his family on the via Mancini and via Pisanelli fronts. He died in 1940 and left the house and his collection to the state; the building came into public life after the death of Lucia Andersen in 1978, and the museum opened on 19 December 1999. The sculptures were carved for the World Centre of Communication that Andersen and Ernest Hébrard published in 1913. The Ministero della Cultura's Visitatori e introiti dei musei gives 10,803 visitors in 2018.

places.name: Teatro Olimpico
places.address: Piazza Gentile da Fabriano 17, 00196 Roma RM
places.summary: A theatre of 1,410 seats, 966 in the raked stalls and 444 in the horseshoe gallery, with a stage about 10 metres deep by 12 metres wide, a removable timber floor and an orchestra pit. The block stands between piazza Gentile da Fabriano, lungotevere Flaminio, viale del Vignola and via Giorgio Vasari. The theatre's own site gives box-office hours of 9.30 to 13.00 and 14.00 to 18.30, Monday to Friday, and a summer closure from 25 July to 23 August. The Accademia Filarmonica Romana is the resident institution and stages most of its events here.
places.history: The block was built in 1935 and 1936 by the firm Garbarino, Sciaccaluga e Mezzacane for the Società Generale Immobiliare, which had bought the property from the Banca Commerciale Italiana in 1935. It ran as the Cine-Teatro Olimpico from 1936, mainly as a cinema with avanspettacolo in the intervals; the Accademia Filarmonica Romana leased it after the Second World War; Teatro Olimpico s.p.a. was formed in 1980 and bought the building, and the name and the programme became Teatro Olimpico in 1981. The building is late-Rationalist: reinforced concrete, with a travertine plinth and travertine window surrounds. On 4 March 1965 Pierre Boulez conducted here the Italian premiere of Stravinsky's Abraham and Isaac and the European premiere of his Elegy for J.F.K. The Accademia itself was founded in Rome in 1821 by amateur musicians led by Raffaele Muti Papazzurri, was made an official institution of the Papal States in 1824, and is a non-profit body under a presidential decree of 7 February 1969.

places.name: Basilica di Santa Croce a Via Flaminia
places.summary: A neo-Romanesque and neo-Byzantine basilica and a parish church, on via Guido Reni. It adjoins MAXXI, which was built on the barracks site next to it. Inside is a modern embroidered and jewelled reproduction of the Constantinian labarum. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The engineer Aristide Leonori built the church at the wish of Pius X to mark the sixteenth centenary of the Edict of Milan of 313. Works began on 17 October 1912 and the church opened on 29 December 1913; Giuseppe Palica, titular archbishop of Philippi and vicegerent of the diocese of Rome, consecrated it on 21 May 1918. It was raised to a parish on 19 March 1914 by the apostolic constitution Quod iam pridem and entrusted to the Stimmatine fathers. Paul VI made it a minor basilica in 1964, and since 5 February 1965 it has been the seat of the cardinalatial title Santa Croce in Via Flaminia, which Paul VI instituted. Those are ranks conferred by the Holy See on its own church.

places.name: Palazzo Marina
places.summary: A state building owned by the Ministry of Defence, in the quartiere Flaminio: seat of the coordinating department of the Regia Marina from its opening and today of the Navy, and home to the Navy's central library. It has two main entrances, one on piazza della Marina off via Flaminia and one on lungotevere delle Navi, with a service entrance on via Domenico Alberto Azuni. It is a working ministry building. No source states public opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The Ministry of the Navy commissioned the building from the architect Giulio Magni; the commission dates from 1912, which is why the design keeps Roman Liberty, barocchetto and eclectic elements. It was inaugurated on 28 October 1928. The site covers 31,000 square metres, of which 11,500 are built over and 4,580 are courtyards and gardens; the building is 28 metres high and 142 metres long, with six storeys and an attic and about 750 rooms. The river-front entrance is flanked by the anchors of the Austro-Hungarian battleships Tegetthoff, on the left, and Viribus Unitis, on the right; the elevations are brick and travertine, with reliefs, sculpture and glass on marine themes.

places.name: Monumento a Giacomo Matteotti (L'idea, la morte)
places.address: Lungotevere Arnaldo da Brescia, 00192 Roma RM
places.summary: An abstract bronze by Iorio Vivarelli on lungotevere Arnaldo da Brescia: a tall slender spire rising from a tangle at its base, on the small semicircular green plot at the Scalo de Pinedo, which it adjoins. A plaque facing the road carries words attributed to Matteotti at his death.
places.history: Giacomo Matteotti, deputy and secretary of the Partito Socialista Unitario, was seized by a fascist squad on 10 June 1924. The monument was funded by a private subscription promoted by the Partito Socialista Italiano and was unveiled in 1974, the fiftieth anniversary of the killing.

places.name: Scalo de Pinedo
places.address: Lungotevere Arnaldo da Brescia, 00192 Roma RM
places.summary: A river port on the Tiber at lungotevere Arnaldo da Brescia, owned by Roma Capitale and long disused as a port. The Monumento a Giacomo Matteotti stands on the green plot beside it.
places.history: It was built at the end of the 19th century to replace the Porto di Ripetta, which was demolished in the same years for the muraglioni flood embankments; the new landing reproduced the 18th-century design of the old one by Alessandro Specchi. Romasegreta gives this account. Rome's 1909 master plan changed the area's designation from industrial-artisanal to residential, and the landing lost its function within a few years of opening.

places.name: Piazza Perin del Vaga
places.address: Piazza Perin del Vaga, 00196 Roma RM
places.summary: An elliptical square, now a pedestrian island, ringed by neo-Renaissance residential blocks and with two travertine dolphin fountains at its sides. It runs between piazza Melozzo da Forlì and the junction of via Girolamo Muziano with via Masolino da Panicale. Roma Capitale's own news item about the square places it in the II Municipio.
places.history: The square was laid out in the 1920s as part of the ICP Flaminio II public housing scheme, already provided for in Rome's 1909 master plan, with lots by Mario De Renzi (lot I) and Alessandro Limongelli (lots II and III) and the outer buildings by Giuseppe Wittinch and Tito Bruner. The quartiere's own entry dates the Case ICP Flaminio II to 1925-27; the attributions are given by ArchiDiAP. The requalification of the square as a pedestrian island, run by Roma Servizi per la Mobilità, was inaugurated in 2019, and Roma Capitale announced it in a news item of 12 July 2019.

places.name: Lungotevere Flaminio
places.summary: The stretch of embankment road running from piazzale delle Belle Arti to ponte Duca d'Aosta, lined with period palazzine. Rowing clubs occupy several of the riverside plots; the Circolo Canottieri Roma is at lungotevere Flaminio 39.
places.history: Among the buildings along it is the Cavalieri di Colombo foundation's, designed by Bruno Ernesto Lapadula in 1934.

places.name: Lungotevere delle Navi
places.summary: The stretch of embankment road running from ponte Giacomo Matteotti to piazzale delle Belle Arti. It is named for the Navy, whose ministry building, Palazzo Marina, stands on it and has one of its two main entrances here.
places.history: The street was instituted by a governor's deliberation of 7 May 1928.

places.name: Lungotevere Grande Ammiraglio Thaon di Revel
places.address: Lungotevere Grande Ammiraglio Thaon di Revel, Roma RM
places.summary: The stretch of embankment road running from ponte Duca d'Aosta to via Flaminia. Its official form is lungotevere Grande A.glio Thaon di Revel, which is how it appears on the street plates and in the street register.
places.history: It is named for Paolo Thaon di Revel, chief of naval staff in the First World War.

places.name: Lungotevere Arnaldo da Brescia
places.address: Lungotevere Arnaldo da Brescia, 00192 Roma RM
places.summary: Lungotevere Arnaldo da Brescia runs from via Ferdinando di Savoia to ponte Matteotti, through the rione Campo Marzio and the quartiere Flaminio. The Scalo de Pinedo and the Monumento a Giacomo Matteotti, on the green plot beside the landing, are addressed to it.
places.history: The street's own article names both the rione and the quartiere, and its infobox carries the two together.

places.name: Ponte Duca d'Aosta
places.summary: A bridge over the Tiber connecting the quartieri Flaminio and Della Vittoria; it lies in both. It is reinforced concrete faced entirely in Tivoli travertine, 222.3 metres long and 30 metres wide, of which 21 metres of carriageway and two footways of 4 metres, carried on three segmental arches.
places.history: A bridge in this position was foreseen in Del Debbio's 1927 scheme for the Foro Mussolini, as its scenographic entrance from Flaminio. The Ministry of Public Works tendered a competition in 1935 which drew 18 entries, among them Ballio Morpurgo, Aschieri, Vaccaro and Del Debbio; Vincenzo Fasolo won it, with the structural engineer Aurelio Aureli. Work began on 21 June 1936 and the bridge was inaugurated on 26 March 1939.

places.name: Ponte della Musica-Armando Trovajoli
places.summary: A bridge over the Tiber between the quartieri Della Vittoria and Flaminio, slung between lungotevere Flaminio and lungotevere Maresciallo Cadorna; it lies in both quartieri. Steel and reinforced concrete, 22 metres wide, it carries cycles, pedestrians and public transport, and no other traffic.
places.history: A bridge here was already in the 1929 master plan. An international competition in 2000 was won by Buro Happold with the engineer Davood Liaghat and Kit Powell-Williams Architects; the bridge was built between 2008 and 2011 and inaugurated in May 2011 as the ponte della Musica, and was renamed for Armando Trovajoli on 30 May 2013. Roma Capitale's own news items carry both dates.

places.name: Ponte del Risorgimento
places.summary: A bridge joining piazzale delle Belle Arti to piazza Monte Grappa, in the quartieri Flaminio and Della Vittoria; it lies in both. It is 159.10 metres long and 20.95 metres wide, carried on a single very flat arch with a rise of about 10 metres, and four inscriptions are cast into its parapets.
places.history: It was built between 1909 and 1911 by Giovanni Antonio Porcheddu, then sole Italian licensee of François Hennebique's patent, with the engineers Chiera, Giaj and Parvopassu and with Hennebique himself supervising, and was inaugurated on 11 May 1911 by mayor Ernesto Nathan during the celebrations of the fiftieth anniversary of Rome as capital. The north parapet reads «Ponte in cemento armato ad un'unica arcata di 100 metri di corda con freccia di 10 metri» and «Costruito con sistema Hennebique dalla Società Porcheddu Ing. G.A.»; the south parapet reads «Inaugurato l'11 maggio del 1911 nel cinquantenario della proclamazione di Roma Capitale d'Italia» and «Dall'amministrazione popolare cittadina al Risorgimento Italiano».

places.name: Villa romana dell'Auditorium e Museo Archeologico
places.address: Viale Pietro de Coubertin, 00196 Roma RM
places.summary: A Roman suburban villa excavated on viale Pietro de Coubertin, with a small archaeological museum for the finds. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina, which runs the museum, opens its account of the site with the words «Nel quartiere Flaminio, durante i lavori per la realizzazione dell'Auditorium progettato da Renzo Piano, nel 1995 vennero alla luce i resti di una grande villa suburbana». The Sovrintendenza gives entry as ingresso libero, free of charge. The remains are seen from the terrace between the Sala Santa Cecilia and the Sala Sinopoli, and the finds are shown in the museum under the cavea. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The Sovrintendenza Capitolina puts the excavated area at about 2,500 square metres; the structures emerged four metres down and survive at foundation level. It records continuous occupation from the second half of the 6th century BC to the 2nd century AD, when the site was abandoned, probably because of the Tiber's floods. A modest farm of the 6th century BC was enlarged in the 5th into a rich rural villa round a central court, with a well-preserved olive press whose pressing surface is cut from a squared block of cappellaccio; a roofed court followed in the late 4th or early 3rd century, together with an eaves tile decorated with the bearded head of a river god identifiable as Achelous; an atrium with impluvium, bedrooms and tablinum was built between the mid-3rd and the 2nd century; and the villa was enlarged again in the Augustan age behind a heavy reticulate wall.

places.name: Chiesa di Sant'Andrea del Vignola
places.summary: A small votive chapel on via Flaminia, also called Sant'Andrea a via Flaminia; its own article places it in the quartiere Flaminio. It is a brick parallelepiped with a peperino façade articulated by pilasters under a triangular pediment; inside are a rectangular hall and a rectangular apse, with an oval half-dome carried on an internal oval cornice. It is a subsidiary place of worship of the parish of Sant'Eugenio. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: It was built about 1553 to a design by Jacopo Barozzi da Vignola for Julius III, inside the grounds of his suburban villa, the Villa Giulia, as a votive chapel marking his escape from Rome on 30 November, St Andrew's day, during the Sack of 1527. It was partly restored between 1826 and 1830, with Giuseppe Valadier involved; the polychrome floor was restored in 1950 under the architect Zander; the dome was re-clad in lead in 1977 and returned to coccio pesto in the 1990s.

places.name: Oratorio di Sant'Andrea a Ponte Milvio
places.summary: A rectangular 15th-century oratory on via Flaminia, the road that runs on to ponte Milvio; it is also called Sant'Andrea a Ponte Molle, and its own article places it in the quartiere Flaminio. The Piccolomini arms are over the door. A small cemetery for foreigners who died on pilgrimage surrounds it, and some wall tablets and an ossuary survive, the ossuary's entrance in the middle of the little garden. It is today a subsidiary place of worship of the parish of Santa Croce a via Flaminia. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The oratory was built beside an aedicule put up by Pius II to commemorate 11 April 1462, when the pope went out to meet Cardinal Bessarione carrying the head of the apostle Andrew, a relic saved by Thomas Palaiologos, despot of Patras, brought to Ancona, then overland to Narni and down the Tiber. Pius V granted the oratory to the archconfraternity of the Trinità dei Pellegrini in 1566. The aedicule, with its travertine base, four alabaster colonnettes with Ionic capitals and Attic bases and a small dome, is attributed to Francesco del Borgo; Manodori gives the statue of St Andrew beneath it to Paolo Taccone in 1463, while Armellini gives it to Varrone and Niccolò of Florence, pupils of Filarete.

places.name: Biblioteca Flaminia
places.summary: The Biblioteca Flaminia, on via Cesare Fracassini, is a branch of the Biblioteche di Roma municipal network. OpenStreetMap places it at number 9. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: No source states a history of the branch.

entries.name: MAXXI - Museo nazionale delle arti del XXI secolo
entries.note: Zaha Hadid's scheme was chosen from 273 competition entries at the end of February 1999 and the museum opened in 2010, on the site of the ex caserma Montello.

entries.name: Piazza Alighiero Boetti
entries.note: MAXXI's forecourt is free and stays open to the public outside the museum's opening hours, with works displayed in it.

entries.name: Museo Hendrik Christian Andersen
entries.note: The sculptor's own palazzina and studio of 1922 to 1925, left to the state at his death in 1940 and opened as a museum on 19 December 1999.

entries.name: Teatro Olimpico
entries.note: A 1,410-seat theatre of 1935 to 1936, home to the Accademia Filarmonica Romana, where Pierre Boulez conducted Stravinsky's Elegy for J.F.K. on 4 March 1965.

entries.name: Basilica di Santa Croce a Via Flaminia
entries.note: Aristide Leonori built it for Pius X to mark the sixteenth centenary of the Edict of Milan; it opened on 29 December 1913 and adjoins MAXXI.

entries.name: Palazzo Marina
entries.note: Giulio Magni's Navy ministry of 1912, inaugurated on 28 October 1928; the river entrance is flanked by the anchors of the Tegetthoff and the Viribus Unitis.

entries.name: Villa romana dell'Auditorium e Museo Archeologico
entries.note: About 2,500 square metres of a suburban villa occupied from the 6th century BC to the 2nd century AD, found in 1995; the Sovrintendenza gives entry as free.

entries.name: Monumento a Giacomo Matteotti (L'idea, la morte)
entries.note: Iorio Vivarelli's bronze spire, unveiled in 1974 on the fiftieth anniversary of the killing of the socialist deputy seized on 10 June 1924.

entries.name: Scalo de Pinedo
entries.note: A disused river landing built at the end of the 19th century to replace the Porto di Ripetta, reproducing Alessandro Specchi's 18th-century design.

entries.name: Piazza Perin del Vaga
entries.note: An elliptical square with two travertine dolphin fountains, laid out in the 1920s with the ICP Flaminio II housing and pedestrianised in 2019.

entries.name: Lungotevere Arnaldo da Brescia
entries.note: The embankment from via Ferdinando di Savoia to ponte Matteotti, through the rione Campo Marzio and the quartiere Flaminio, carrying the Scalo de Pinedo.

entries.name: Ponte del Risorgimento
entries.note: Porcheddu built it on Hennebique's patent in 1909 to 1911 and Ernesto Nathan inaugurated it on 11 May 1911; four inscriptions are cast into its parapets.

entries.name: Chiesa di Sant'Andrea del Vignola
entries.note: Vignola built this votive chapel about 1553 for Julius III, inside the grounds of his suburban villa, to mark the pope's escape from the Sack of 1527.

entries.name: Oratorio di Sant'Andrea a Ponte Milvio
entries.note: A 15th-century oratory built beside the aedicule Pius II raised for the arrival of the head of the apostle Andrew on 11 April 1462.

links.note: The quartiere across via Flaminia, holding Villa Borghese, the Galleria Borghese and Villa Giulia. Piazzale Flaminio is divided between the two.
The neighbour past viale Maresciallo Pilsudski, which holds the Auditorium Parco della Musica, the Stadio Flaminio and ponte Milvio.
The rione inside the Aurelian Walls to the south, holding Piazza del Popolo and Porta del Popolo, and sharing lungotevere Arnaldo da Brescia.
Across the Tiber by ponte Giacomo Matteotti and ponte Pietro Nenni.
